newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN MP CRITICISES EU OSTRICH BAN.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN MP CRITICISES EU OSTRICH BAN.

text.p: A parliamentarian from South Africa's ruling African National Congress on Friday condemned the European Union ban on South African ostrich meat over health fears as irresponsible and inappropriate.

"It is obvious that the action of the EU was based on their trying to equate this outbreak with the English Mad Cow disease," Reggie Oliphant, who represents the capital of South Africa's ostrich industry in the town of Oudtshoorn, said in a statement.
"Such an equation is quite obviously completely eroneous," he said.
"This decision directly affects 1,500 job opportunities in the area. It will have an unwarranted and unnecessary negative impact on the entire economic system including tourism," Oliphant said.

"I appeal to all concerned in the ostrich industry to assist me and the government to ensure that this ban is not put into effect, as there is no foundation to it at all...it is both inappropriate and irresponsible."

The EU on Thursday banned imports of ostrich meat or live ostriches from South Africa because of an outbreak of Congo fever among ostrich abattoir workers in Oudtshoorn last month. One worker died and 16 others were treated in hospital.
Ostrich meat gained popularity in Europe after the outbreak of Mad Cow disease in cattle which scientists said might be passed on to humans who ate beef from infected animals.
The EU ban is due to be reviewed in February, or sooner if new evidence emerges about the effect on humans who eat ostriches which have been bitten by the ticks that carry Congo fever.

A spokesman for the Little Karoo Cooperative in Oudtshoorn, which produces about 80 percent of world ostrich products, said the cooperative had decided to make funds available so research into the health implications of eating ostrich meat could begin immediately.
He said the abattoir, which was closed last month when the disease broke out there, would reopen on November 27 despite the EU ban.

Hides and feathers, which together account for 80 percent of the value of an ostrich, are not affected by the ban. Meat from slaughtered ostriches would be frozen for possible future consumption, the spokesman said.
